premise: A team wants a mailbox inventory it can test on made-up data before reading a live system.
caption: Request for Devin
before: My practice kit contains mailboxes.csv. Build the read-only PowerShell inventory from that file. Keep user and shared rows, sort by address and run the five kit checks. Which rows stay out?
after: First run: The four addresses sort as accounts@example.test, box-a@example.test, box-b@example.test and box-c@example.test. The types in order are shared, user, shared, user. Second run: All five checks pass with the original. The backward sort fails. Team, Blue stays in one name field and Café Desk keeps its accent. Room and device rows stay out.
why: A deliberately reversed sort proves the report test can actually catch an error.
rescue: A practice result can be mistaken for a live tenant test. Ask for a closer check.
rescuePrompt: Label each run with its actual data source and identify which test failed when the sort was reversed.
try:
1. A branch is a separate line of work in the same project. Start a Devin session on a new branch of your practice project. Prepare the sample in “Unzip the sample kit” first.
2. Give Devin the worked request about mailboxes.csv and the practice kit. Read the plan and the script changes. Use the kit on your computer in practice mode.
3. A CSV is a plain-text table with a row on each line. Run the kit's Test-Inventory.ps1 in practice mode. Open the CSV and read its addresses in order.
4. In a spare copy, reverse the sort and run the five checks again.

premise: A report labels usage near a limit. The exact cutoff is easy to get wrong.
caption: Request for Devin
after: First run: 79 is normal. Both 80 and 81 are watch. Second run: The current code returns normal. You have found a missing rule for a bad percentage.
why: An impossible percentage getting an ordinary label exposes a missing input check.
rescue: If 80 is labeled normal, ask for a targeted follow-up.
rescuePrompt: Look for > where the sample says >=.
try:
1. A branch is a separate line of work in the same project. Start a Devin session on a new branch of your practice project. Prepare the sample in “Start a practice session” first.
2. Send the request about percent.
3. Run label on 79, 80 and 81. Mark where the printed word first changes.
4. Run label(-1) as a separate trial. Discuss whether the word normal makes sense for that input.

premise: A location name contains a comma that belongs inside one CSV column.
caption: Request for Devin
before:
My CSV includes the quoted name “North, West”. The starter splits on every comma. Give the field count on each line before and after a fix that understands quotes.

sample.csv:
id,name
m1,"North, West"
m2,East
parser.py starter: print([len(line.rstrip().split(",")) for line in open("sample.csv")])
after: First run: The broken count list is 2, 3, 2. The fixed list is 2, 2, 2. Second run: The new row has two fields. The second is an empty string. North, West stays together on its own row.
why: A comma inside quotes belongs to the name and must not create a third column.
rescue: If North and West still show up as separate columns, ask for a targeted follow-up.
rescuePrompt: See whether the script still splits each line by hand.
try:
1. A branch is a separate line of work in the same project. Start a Devin session on a new branch of your practice project. Prepare the sample in “Start a practice session” first.
2. Send the request about North.
3. Run the small parser on the file. Count fields before and after the repair.
4. Add m3,"" as a new row. Check its two fields and see whether the second field stays empty.

premise: A report command should find its input even when someone starts it in a different folder.
caption: Request for Devin
before:
My cleanlab folder contains report.py and the West/East count file. Make the report find its data beside the script.

site,count
West,3
East,5

What total prints when I start it from the parent folder?
after: First run: From inside cleanlab, python3 report.py prints 8. from the parent folder, python3 cleanlab/report.py also prints 8. Second run: Both complete copies print 8. The copy missing its input stops with an error. West 3 + East 5 = 8 from both starting folders.
why: Running the same report from another folder reveals whether it can find its own input.
rescue: If the second command cannot find rows.csv, ask for a targeted follow-up.
rescuePrompt: Explain how report.py locates rows.csv when the caller starts in the parent folder. Test both working directories.
try:
1. Open the cleanlab practice folder in Devin and give it the report request. Review the change to the file path.
2. Run python3 report.py inside cleanlab. Go to its parent and run python3 cleanlab/report.py. Compare the totals.
3. Copy the folder, remove the sample data from that copy, and run its report again. Read the last line.

premise: The same ID appears with different spacing and capitalization.
caption: Request for Devin
after: First run: The supplied list gives just a1. Before the repair extra spaces create extra entries. Second run: The new group gives b2 and c3 once each. The empty group gives an empty list.
why: Trimming before comparing IDs keeps a space-only entry from claiming an extra place in the list.
rescue: If you cannot see the spaces, ask for a targeted follow-up.
rescuePrompt: Print the representation of each input string so leading, trailing and space-only values are visible.
try:
1. A branch is a separate line of work in the same project. Start a Devin session on a new branch of your practice project. Prepare the sample in “Start a practice session” first.
2. Send the request about IDs.
3. Run unique on the original list. Inspect spaces and case before accepting the fix.
4. Try B2 and b2 with outside spaces, plus two spellings of C3. Also test an empty list.

premise: The next shift needs a written rule for counting valid readings and flagging missing ones.
caption: Request for Devin
before:
Turn the ID,Count check into a short recipe another session can reuse. A blank needs a look but a zero is valid. Put the rule in training/REVIEW.md and include the count, total and skipped IDs.

ID,Count
a,3
b,0
c,

Which rows go into the total?
after: First run: Rows a and b are valid, even though b is zero. Their sum is 3. Row c needs a look. Second run: Two rows count. The sum is 9. Row x needs a look. The first sum is 3 + 0 = 3. The second is 8 + 1 = 9.
why: The second session can read the saved rule. That is how it knows zero belongs in the count.
rescue: If b disappears, ask for a targeted follow-up.
rescuePrompt: Add a line to the recipe showing that zero is a real count.
try:
1. A branch is a separate line of work in the same project. Start a Devin session on a new branch of your practice project. Prepare the sample in “Start a practice session” first.
2. Send the request about Count.
3. Run the saved rule on a, b and c. Compare the zero row with the blank row.
4. Open a fresh session and give it only the recipe and the second sheet with x=-2, y=8 and z=1.

premise: A score page should remember its earlier entries after a reload.
caption: Request for Devin
before:
Build a score page that remembers positive and negative turns on this device. Add the two sample turns, reload and try a blank submission.

Opening score: 0
First change: +12
Second change: -5
After reload: blank submission

Which score survives?
after: First run: The total starts at 0, then becomes 12, then 7. Reload shows 7. Second run: The total stays 7 both times. The hint asks for a number. 0 + 12 − 5 = 7.
why: Reloading tests saved points, and a blank submission tests input handling without erasing them.
rescue: If reload starts from zero, ask for a targeted follow-up.
rescuePrompt: Check whether the tool reads its saved value when it opens, before drawing the score.
try:
1. A branch is a separate line of work in the same project. Start a Devin session on a new branch of your practice project. Prepare the sample in “Start a practice session” first.
2. Send the request about score.
3. Apply +12 and then -5. Reload the page and read the saved score.
4. Submit a blank entry. Read the hint. Reload the same address once more.

premise: A repeated issue notice should lead back to its existing task.
caption: Request for Devin
before:
For each issue and revision, start just one practice task. Separate a repeated delivery ID from a new delivery for the same work.

delivery,issue,revision
d1,T21,r1
d1,T21,r1
d2,T21,r1
d3,T21,r2

How many tasks do the four rows create?
after: First run: The four events produce two tasks: T21/r1 and T21/r2. Second run: Old deliveries keep their tasks after restart. The new issue makes the third task.
why: An issue and revision identify the job even when the delivery system repeats a notification.
rescue: If a restart makes extra tasks, ask for a targeted follow-up.
rescuePrompt: Check that both runs open the same database file and use the same two-part match.
try:
1. A branch is a separate line of work in the same project. Start a Devin session on a new branch of your practice project. Prepare the sample in “Start a practice session” first.
2. Send the request about revision.
3. Feed the four delivery events to the test. Count tasks by issue and revision.
4. Run the first three rows, close the program, then run the full list with the same database. Add d4,T22,r1.

premise: A reviewer needs to compare the access the team approved with the access it actually found.
caption: Request for Devin
before:
My approved and observed lists pair a role with a resource. Ignore exact repeats.

Approved: Reader/reports, Maintainer/app.
Observed: Reader/reports, Reader/reports, Reader/app.

Which Reader grant is extra, and which approved grant is missing?
after: First run: Reader/app is extra. Maintainer/app is missing. Reader/reports is repeated. Second run: The lists now match. The repeat also disappears.
why: One list shows what is allowed. The other shows what exists. Checking both reveals what is extra and what is missing.
rescue: If the missing pair is absent from the report, ask for a targeted follow-up.
rescuePrompt: Compare approved against observed in a separate pass.
try:
1. A branch is a separate line of work in the same project. Start a Devin session on a new branch of your practice project. Prepare the sample in “Start a practice session” first.
2. Send the request about Reader.
3. Compare the approved and observed lists. Mark repeats, extras and missing pairs separately.
4. Replace the repeat Reader/reports with Maintainer/app and remove Reader/app. Run again.

premise: A team wants the cost of each accepted change, including the time spent on retries.
caption: Request for Devin
before:
Our pretend sessions used units against changes P1 and P2. Give total units per accepted change, counting the cost of failed tries too.

session,units,pr,accepted
s1,4,P1,yes
s2,2,P1,yes
s3,3,P2,no
s4,1,,no

What if none were accepted?
after: First run: The rows use 10 units. Only P1 is accepted. That gives 10 units per accepted change. Second run: Total use is still 10. Accepted changes are 0. The rate has no value because you cannot divide by zero. (4 + 2 + 3 + 1) ÷ 1 = 10 units per accepted change.
why: Two accepted sessions for the same change still have only one accepted change between them.
rescue: If you get 5 units per win, ask for a targeted follow-up.
rescuePrompt: Check whether you counted two yes rows for P1.
try:
1. A branch is a separate line of work in the same project. Start a Devin session on a new branch of your practice project. Prepare the sample in “Start a practice session” first.
2. Send the request about P1.
3. Add the units from all four sessions. Count different accepted changes before dividing.
4. Set every accepted marker to no and repeat the report.

premise: Two records look alike on a clock but may fall on opposite sides of a reporting window.
caption: Request for Devin
before:
Find records inside the stated UTC time window, including the first moment and leaving out the last. Give each known local time as UTC.

A 2026-11-01T01:15:00-04:00
B 2026-11-01T01:15:00-05:00
C 2026-11-01T06:30:00+00:00
D 2026-11-01T01:20:00
Window 05:15Z through 06:30Z on Nov 1.

Which record is too vague to place?
after: First run: A is 05:15 UTC and B is 06:15 UTC. Both count. C is exactly at the end. D has no offset. Second run: Now only B is in the window. The gap from A to B is still 60 minutes. 06:15 minus 05:15 is 1 × 60 = 60 minutes.
why: The time offset tells how far a clock is from UTC, the shared time standard. The two clocks show the same hour but mark different moments.
rescue: If C is counted, ask for a targeted follow-up.
rescuePrompt: Change the test for the end time from at or before to strictly before.
try:
1. A branch is a separate line of work in the same project. Start a Devin session on a new branch of your practice project. Prepare the sample in “Start a practice session” first.
2. Send the request about UTC.
3. UTC is one shared clock. It lets you compare times from different places. Place the four times in the UTC window. Record each time that lacks its date or offset.
4. Move only the start to 05:15:01 UTC. Run the same checks.

premise: A job was saved before its first reply timed out. A retry might accidentally start it again.
caption: Request for Devin
before:
Creating T9 once saves S1 but its reply times out. Look up T9 before doing more work. Count create calls.

Create T9: store S1, then throw timeout.
Lookup T9: one match S1.
Create call counter begins at zero.

What should happen when the lookup finds zero or multiple matches?
after: First run: One match returns S1. The create count is 1, even after restart. Second run: The result says which two IDs conflict. It makes no new task.
why: Looking up the saved job after a lost reply prevents the retry from creating a second task.
rescue: If the second run creates a task, ask for a targeted follow-up.
rescuePrompt: Check that it reads the saved unknown result before it tries to start anything.
try:
1. A branch is a separate line of work in the same project. Start a Devin session on a new branch of your practice project. Prepare the sample in “Start a practice session” first.
2. Send the request about T9.
3. Run the timeout test. Inspect the lookup and count how often create actually ran.
4. Change the lookup so T9 has both S1 and S2. Try the check again.

premise: Old and new report files use different names for the same count.
caption: Request for Devin
after: First run: The old record, the new record and the equal pair each give 2. The mismatched pair fails. Second run: The old record still gives 2. The reader still rejects count 2 paired with total 3.
why: When both field names are present, comparing them catches a disagreement an old reader would overlook.
rescue: If the reader chooses one number from a conflicting pair, ask for a targeted follow-up.
rescuePrompt: Add the check for two fields before selecting a field.
try:
1. A branch is a separate line of work in the same project. Start a Devin session on a new branch of your practice project. Prepare the sample in “Start a practice session” first.
2. Send the request about count.
3. Try the old, new, matching and conflicting records. Record the reply for each.
4. Put the old writer back and keep the new reader. Read its output once more.

premise: A report has a known good total. An incomplete update must leave that file usable.
caption: Request for Devin
before:
My last saved total is 7. I need a new report covering both North and South. Protect the saved copy when a region is absent. Include a pretend stop just before replacing current.json.

current.json contains {"total":7}
manifest: North,South
partial input: North=4
good input: North=4,South=5

Which run can replace it?
after: First run: A file naming only North leaves 7. A forced stop with both rows ready also leaves the old file exactly as it was. Second run: The full set writes 9. The bad repeat leaves that good 9 unchanged. The complete total is 4 + 5 = 9.
why: South is missing from the first set. A correct number for North alone cannot replace the full report.
rescue: If the old report vanishes, ask for a targeted follow-up.
rescuePrompt: Check whether the program opens it for writing before all the checks finish.
try:
1. A branch is a separate line of work in the same project. Start a Devin session on a new branch of your practice project. Prepare the sample in “Start a practice session” first.
2. Send the request about North.
3. Try the North-only input and the simulated stop. Reopen current.json after each.
4. Run with North=4 and South=5. Then try two North rows and no South.

premise: A mail move has a completion target and a separate approval requirement.
caption: Request for Devin
before:
The move needs 95% completion and owner approval. Use the North and South counts and the owner's note. Give each status and show exactly what proof is missing.

Manifest North,South. R1 North 48/50. R2 South 47/50. A1 owner: review pending.
after: First run: The starting numbers are 95 of 100, but A1 says review pending. The result is HOLD. Second run: Approval makes the complete set pass at exactly 95%. Both bad sets stop, and the test directions work for the next reader. (48 + 47) ÷ (50 + 50) × 100 = 95 percent.
why: An approval and a passing rate are two separate requirements for marking the move ready.
rescue: If 51/50 gives a pass, ask for a targeted follow-up.
rescuePrompt: Compare completed with attempted for each group before adding the groups.
try:
1. A branch is a separate line of work in the same project. Start a Devin session on a new branch of your practice project. Prepare the sample in “Start a practice session” first.
2. Send the request about approval.
3. Run the check on both regions with the original owner note. Read its decision.
4. Change A1 to approved. Then separately test missing South and a restored South at 51/50. Follow the README in a fresh folder.

premise: An engineer wants to run a project’s tests. The README names the command, so Devin’s answer can be checked without editing anything.
caption: Practice request
before: Inspect the practice repository without editing it. Which file names the test command, and what command does it give? Point to the line so I can check it.
after: First run: README names python3 test_desk.py. Second run: The new revision names python3 test_gate.py. The earlier desk command belongs to the first revision.
why: A read-only first question shows which repository and revision Devin is actually reading.
rescue: If the command is invented, ask for its location.
rescuePrompt: Show the exact README line in the selected revision before naming the test command.
try:
1. A repository keeps project files and their saved history. Select a scratch repository in Devin with a README stating “Run checks with python3 test_desk.py.” Start in Ask.
2. Give Devin Ask the lookup request. Compare the command it reports with the line in README.
3. Change the README yourself to name test_gate.py. Start a new Ask session against the updated revision.

premise: A team needs to locate a report’s input before deciding whether the project needs an edit.
caption: Practice request
before: Where does the report get its input according to the README? Find the evidence in this repo and stop at that answer. No file change is needed.
after: First run: The reply from Ask names fixture.csv and creates no patch. Second run: README gains Test command: python3 report.py. No other file changes.
why: Picking a read-only question for Ask avoids launching an edit just to locate a filename.
rescue: If a lookup produces a patch, ask for a narrower task.
rescuePrompt: Report where the input is documented. Leave the repository as you found it.
try:
1. A repository keeps project files and their saved history. A commit is a saved checkpoint in a project. In a practice project, put this line in README: “report.py reads fixture.csv”. Save it as a commit and send that commit to the practice branch. Select that repository in Devin Ask once its index includes the line.
2. Give Ask the request. Check its answer against README without making edits.
3. In Devin Agent select the same branch. Ask for a plan to add the separate line Test command: python3 report.py to README. Approve the one-line plan and ask Agent to apply it. Read the old and new lines in the change view.

premise: A library help page needs one correct example of its renewal rule.
caption: Practice request
before: Plan a tiny change to loans.txt that illustrates the renewal rule with one allowed case. Keep the rule itself intact. Which file needs to change?
after: First run: First example allows one renewal with nobody waiting. Second run: Second example refuses renewal when a borrower waits. The earlier example still covers a loan with no waiting borrower.
why: A rule with a passing case and a refusing case is easier to review than a rewritten paragraph.
rescue: If both borrowers renew, ask for the blocking condition.
rescuePrompt: Apply the original waiting-borrower condition to the second example and retain the original rule.
try:
1. A repository keeps project files and their saved history. Choose a practice repository in Devin Agent. Start with a file called loans.txt containing “Renew once if no one is waiting.”.
2. Send the renewal request to Agent, read the plan, and compare the proposed edit with loans.txt.
3. A diff shows which lines changed. Ask for a waiting-borrower example as a second edit. Review the diff before accepting each change.

premise: A report script needs to find its sample counts when someone runs it from another folder.
caption: Practice request
before: Build a tiny report that finds counts.csv beside its script and prints the total. Which command will let another session run this without a machine-specific path?
after: First run: 2 + 7 = 9 from the project folder. Second run: The parent-folder run also prints 9. Both starts reach the same data file.
why: A reusable environment must not depend on the directory where a terminal happens to start.
rescue: If the second command cannot find its CSV, ask what path it constructed.
rescuePrompt: Locate counts.csv relative to the script and repeat the test from both directories.
try:
1. Prepare a practice repo containing counts.csv with one Count column and values 2 and 7. Start a Devin session from the selected environment.
2. Ask Devin to build the report and run it against counts.csv. Record the working directory and printed sum.
3. Run it from the project folder, then from its parent using the script's path. Inspect both command outputs.

premise: A running total needs to keep earlier entries when a new value is added.
caption: Practice request
before: Create a running score display. It starts at zero, accepts signed whole numbers and keeps all previous turns. Show the score after entries 5 and -2. What is the running score after each entry?
after: First run: 5 − 2 = 3. Second run: Undo removes -2 and restores 5. The previous turn is still on the score sheet.
why: A small follow-up in the same session lets you see whether the agent kept the first behavior.
rescue: If Undo clears all turns, ask for one history entry to be removed.
rescuePrompt: Keep earlier score entries and remove only the newest turn when Undo is pressed.
try:
1. Start a Devin Agent session in a practice folder.
2. Submit the worked request about score, inspect the changed lines, and try the first two signed turns.
3. While reviewing the output, request Undo last turn. Try it once and inspect the changed files.

premise: A guest limit includes the last allowed guest. A test at that exact number can catch a wrong comparison.
caption: Practice request
before: The written rule allows up to and including four guests. Demonstrate the failing boundary test, fix only that comparison, and show the test output on both versions. Which test detects the changed boundary?
after: First run: Four changes from refused to allowed. Second run: Five stays refused. The repaired rule admits four while leaving five outside the limit.
why: Four tests the fix at its cutoff. Five shows that the rule still blocks a guest just outside it.
rescue: If the agent broadens every case, ask for the first disallowed count.
rescuePrompt: Test the value just outside the allowed range and show the comparison in the diff.
try:
1. In a Devin practice repo create gate.py with one line: def allowed(n): return n < 4. Ask the agent for a plan and a test before editing.
2. Have Devin run the boundary test before and after the proposed edit. Read the comparison in the diff.
3. Review the diff. Test five guests after the fix as a control.

premise: Several shifts need to check the same report headers and distinguish a zero from a missing count.
caption: Practice request
before: Draft a reusable report recipe that checks the headers, counts known entries including zero, and gives the sum. Try it on the supplied practice file. Report any missing count by its row ID.
after: First run: 2 known entries with total 2. Second run: 1 known entry with total 2 and b reported missing. The missing value has no part in the sum.
why: A new sample file still needs the same rule for blank counts. That is what makes the recipe worth saving.
rescue: If both files report two known entries, ask how the recipe recognizes a missing value.
rescuePrompt: Mark the status of each Count field before adding it to the report.
try:
1. A CSV is a plain-text table with a row on each line. Prepare a local CSV named counts.csv with the heading ID,Count and rows a,2 and b,0. Open a Devin practice project with playbooks available.
2. Submit the worked request about recipe. Save the agreed recipe and run it on the initial two-row file.
3. Run the same recipe on a file with a,2 and b,empty. Treat the word empty as missing.

premise: One ticket revision arrives twice through separate deliveries. The team needs only one coding job.
caption: Practice request
before: Build a local simulation. Ticket D7 revision one is delivered twice, with a different delivery ID each time. Keep one session per ticket and apply each revision once. Which session records should exist?
after: First run: One session S1 for D7, with revision one recorded once. Second run: S1 contains revisions one and two once each. The session count stays at one.
why: A delivery ID can change on a retry even though the requested work is identical.
rescue: If revision two creates another session for D7, ask for the ticket-to-session lookup.
rescuePrompt: Look up the session by ticket ID. Within that session apply each unseen revision once even when delivery IDs differ.
try:
1. Start a Devin Agent session on a practice branch. Ask for a plan for the local simulation and review its diff.
2. Run the two deliveries using session S1 for D7. Inspect the session list and applied revisions.
3. Append D7 revision two twice. Run both deliveries and inspect S1 again.

premise: A practice account can read a project. The proposed action would also need permission to write.
caption: Practice request
before: Repo grant: read. Project role: reviewer. Requested action: push a change. Explain which permission prevents a push and what useful work can still be done.
after: First run: Push blocked by the read-only repo grant. Second run: Reading README fits the grant. The permission still blocks writes.
why: A project role cannot supply a missing permission at the code host.
rescue: If a reviewer is told to push, ask for the matching repository grant.
rescuePrompt: Evaluate the requested operation against the listed repo grant before describing the project role.
try:
1. In Devin Ask, supply this fictional permission matrix. Use a practice project and leave all grants untouched.
2. Ask Devin Ask to compare the proposed change with the supplied grants. Inspect which permission it cites.
3. Change the request to reading README. Ask for the decision again.

premise: A report needs project files and a file store. Its worker needs to reach both.
caption: Practice request
before: Runner A can read the practice repo. Only Runner B can reach the file store. A report needs both. Show where this deployment path stops and label the missing connection.
after: First run: A lacks the file store and B lacks the project folder. Second run: B can read both inputs needed for this project folderrt. The report needs both the project and the file store.
why: Where a job runs matters when only one machine can reach a required file.
rescue: If the diagram jumps across machines, ask for the input path on the chosen runner.
rescuePrompt: For each input, identify whether the same runner can read it.
try:
1. Use Devin Ask to draw the path of a fictional job. Keep the customer file and all machines fictional.
2. Have Devin map each practice runner to the resources it can reach. Check the proposed job against that map.
3. Give Runner B read access to the practice repo. Redraw the path using B alone.

premise: A caller loses track of a job after starting it. Its saved session ID can help recover the result.
caption: Practice request
before: Model starting an offline mock session. A start returns S4; a status lookup for S4 returns running. Store that ID and poll it without requesting a second session. Show the call sequence. Which request can reuse the first job?
after: First run: One start, followed by status for S4. Second run: Finished on S4. The start count stays at one. The final status belongs to the original session.
why: Keeping the session ID lets a client check progress without paying for another start.
rescue: If a second ID appears, ask for the start-call log.
rescuePrompt: Reuse S4 for every status lookup and show each call in order.
try:
1. Select a practice project in Devin Agent for the local session simulation.
2. Run the mock start and status lookup. Record the returned session ID and count the start calls.
3. Make the next lookup return finished. Inspect the calls and count starts.

premise: Two projects need a Help button renamed. Each proposed edit needs its own test.
caption: Practice request
before: Both projects have a local Help button. Plan a two-project change to the label Guide. Keep a separate test result per project; Shelf already passed and Desk has no result yet. Which project still blocks the fleet? Give the starting release status for both projects.
after: First run: Shelf passed and Desk is untested. Second run: Shelf and Desk each have their own passing result. The two checks name different projects.
why: One successful repository cannot stand in for a second repository's missing result.
rescue: If the fleet is called ready early, ask for separate evidence.
rescuePrompt: List Shelf and Desk separately with the exact test result supplied for each.
try:
1. Select practice projects Shelf and Desk in Devin. Keep each project’s test evidence separate.
2. Send the label-change plan request. Read the separate Shelf and Desk statuses before declaring the release ready.
3. A repository keeps project files and their saved history. Give Devin this update: Desk passed. Update the two-project status note and say whether a project still blocks release.

premise: Several sessions contribute to one proposed fix. Spending is counted even when an edit is declined.
caption: Practice request
before: Session A used 4 units for accepted fix P1. B used 3 on the same P1. C used 2 on a declined fix. What was the cost per distinct accepted fix?
after: First run: (4 + 3 + 2) ÷ 1 = 9 units per accepted fix. Second run: 9 ÷ 2 = 4.5 units per accepted fix. The same nine units now cover two accepted fixes.
why: Nine units bought one accepted fix in the first run. It makes no difference that two sessions worked on that one fix.
rescue: If three sessions become three wins, ask to group by accepted fix ID.
rescuePrompt: List the distinct accepted fix IDs before dividing total units.
try:
1. Start in Devin Ask with the fictional session ledger. Keep estimated cost separate from the number of accepted changes.
2. Ask for the total use and distinct accepted fixes. Check whether retries for P1 are counted correctly.
3. Change C to an accepted separate fix P2 and recompute from the same units.

premise: Optional live extension to the checkout case. Use Devin Agent to build and test the fee ledger.
caption: Practice request
before: Implement a ledger for a practice checkout. Ticket G has one fee of 3 credits. A retry with the same ticket must reuse the recorded fee. Run the retry and show the ledger. Which ledger row carries the charge?
after: First run: The only row is G, 3 credits even after the retry. Second run: The rows are G, 3 and H, 2. Total fees are 3 + 2 = 5 credits.
why: The repeated ticket and the new ticket test opposite sides of the duplicate rule.
rescue: If G is charged twice, ask for the ledger before the retry.
rescuePrompt: Use the ticket identifier to find the existing charge before adding a new fee.
try:
1. Choose a disposable repo in Devin Agent. Ask for the plan and the smallest test for a repeated fee.
2. Run the request with two deliveries for ticket G. Read both the changed code and the actual saved ledger.
3. A diff shows which lines changed. Add ticket H with a 2-credit fee. Review the diff and run both ticket cases again.

premise: A counter should work the same way with a keyboard as it does with a mouse.
caption: Request for Devin
before:
I want one Count button that adds two with a tap or a keyboard press. Give me Reset and a big score.

Start 0. Count button adds 2. Reset returns to 0.

What does a second press do before Reset?
after: First run: Two taps give 2 and then 4. The Reset button gives 0. Second run: The keyboard press gives 2 just like a tap. The Reset button returns to 0. Two presses add 2 + 2 = 4.
why: Checking the keyboard as well as a tap tests whether each way adds exactly one turn's points.
rescue: If Enter adds four, ask for a targeted follow-up.
rescuePrompt: Check whether both the click handler and a second key handler ran for the same press.
try:
1. A branch is a separate line of work in the same project. Start a Devin session on a new branch of your practice project.
2. Send the worked example about Count. Read the proposed changes, then open the page in its browser preview.
3. Tap Count twice. Read the number after each tap, then press Reset.
4. Use the Tab key to move to Count by two. Press Enter once, then press Reset.

premise: A lost-and-found desk needs to match an entire tag even if somebody types extra spaces.
caption: Request for Devin
before:
Make a lost-and-found tag lookup. Match a whole tag after trimming spaces and ignoring case. Give an Unknown tag result for a partial or missing tag and a Clear button.

T1 hat; T2 blue bag; T3 mug.
after: First run: Entering “ t2 ” shows blue bag. T alone shows Unknown tag. Second run: T9 shows Unknown tag. The Clear button empties the field and old result. T1 shows hat.
why: T2 belongs to one item. The letter T starts several tags, so it cannot safely name a bag.
rescue: If T returns all three, ask for a targeted follow-up.
rescuePrompt: Match the whole tag after trimming spaces and normalizing case. A partial tag must stay unknown.
try:
1. A branch is a separate line of work in the same project. Start a Devin session on a new branch of your practice project.
2. Send the worked example about tag. Read the proposed changes, then open the page in its browser preview.
3. Look up “ t2 ” with spaces. Next try just T and read the label.
4. Search T9, then Clear, then T1.

premise: A notification tool has a length rule for the subject line of a message.
caption: Request for Devin
before:
Build a subject checker. Count letters and inside spaces only after trimming the ends. Give Missing at zero, Too short under five and Ready otherwise.

Subjects: Trip; two spaces; Plan update. Minimum length 5 after trimming.

What length appears?
after: First run: Trip gives 4 and Too short. Two spaces gives 0 and Missing. Plan update gives 11 and Ready. Second run: The reported length is 5 and the word is Ready. Plan update has 4 + 1 + 6 = 11 characters. Trimming the spaces leaves five letters in Plans.
why: Counting letters after trimming keeps spaces from satisfying the minimum subject length.
rescue: If a blank is called short, ask for a targeted follow-up.
rescuePrompt: Check for zero length before checking the under-five rule.
try:
1. A branch is a separate line of work in the same project. Start a Devin session on a new branch of your practice project.
2. Send the worked example about subject. Read the proposed changes, then open the page in its browser preview.
3. Check Trip, two spaces, and Plan update. Read the length and status for each.
4. Enter “ Plans ” including the outside spaces.

premise: A short packing quiz needs to count each answer only once.
caption: Request for Devin
before:
My packing quiz lets me choose map, key and bell. Each right pick earns one and a wrong pick costs one. Give the score and let me uncheck everything for another try. Stop at zero if deductions outweigh correct picks.

Choices: map, key, bell. Correct set: map and bell.
after: First run: Picking only map earns 1. Picking all three earns 1 because key costs one point. Second run: The result is 2 of 2 with no wrong picks. The Reset button unchecks all three. Map and bell minus key gives 1 + 1 − 1 = 1.
why: Counting unwanted choices as deductions stops selecting every option from beating the quiz.
rescue: If the score changes on every extra tap of Check, ask for a targeted follow-up.
rescuePrompt: Calculate it from the selected boxes each time.
try:
1. A branch is a separate line of work in the same project. Start a Devin session on a new branch of your practice project.
2. Send the worked example about map. Read the proposed changes, then open the page in its browser preview.
3. Choose only map, then all three items. Read the score after each choice.
4. Try again, then select map and bell only and press Check.

premise: A ticket form must warn the operator before a note exceeds the allowed length.
caption: Request for Devin
before:
Build a note editor with a 12-character limit. Show room left, disable Save when over the limit and keep the last saved note.

Limit 12. Sample “Meet at pier” has 12 characters including spaces.

What happens with a thirteenth character?
after: First run: Typing Meet at pier shows 0 left and allows Save. The saved area shows the phrase. Second run: The extra character shows 1 over. The Save button is off. The previous saved note stays visible in both cases. Meet at pier uses 4 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 4 = 12 characters. One more gives 13, one past the limit.
why: Disabling Save for an overlong note should protect the previous saved text.
rescue: If an over-limit edit changes the saved area, ask for a targeted follow-up.
rescuePrompt: Update that area only when Save succeeds.
try:
1. A branch is a separate line of work in the same project. Start a Devin session on a new branch of your practice project.
2. Send the worked example about note. Read the proposed changes, then open the page in its browser preview.
3. Type Meet at pier and press Save. Check the count and saved words.
4. Add an exclamation point. Try saving. Then erase the draft.

premise: A draw should produce each card once before a fresh deck starts.
caption: Request for Devin
before:
Give me a deck that draws each card once. Add a fixed test order and Reset.

Fixed test deck bell, key, rope, flag.

How many cards remain after each draw, including a draw from the empty deck?
after: First run: Four draws give bell, key, rope and flag in test mode. The remaining counts are 3, 2, 1, 0. Second run: The extra draw cannot create a fifth card. The reset deck starts with bell and 3 remaining. Each legal draw removes one card. After four draws 4 − 4 = 0 remain.
why: Drawing every card once catches repeats that a single lucky draw would miss.
rescue: If a card repeats early, ask for a targeted follow-up.
rescuePrompt: Inspect the remaining deck after each draw. Make sure the picked card has left it.
try:
1. A branch is a separate line of work in the same project. Start a Devin session on a new branch of your practice project.
2. Send the worked example about deck. Read the proposed changes, then open the page in its browser preview.
3. Draw four cards in test mode. Read the deck after each draw.
4. Try Draw again, then New deck. Draw once in the reset test deck.

premise: Two teams take turns in a race, and no further roll should change the winner.
caption: Request for Devin
before:
Build a race using these fixed rolls for Blue and Gold. End the race as soon as someone reaches ten.

Start at 0 for both. Blue rolls 4, Gold 3, Blue 6. Target 10.

Which scores remain when a player presses Roll after the win?
after: First run: Blue reaches 10 on turn three. Gold remains at 3. The winner says Blue. Second run: The extra press has no effect. Restart puts Blue first with 0 to 0. Blue rolls 4 + 6 = 10. Gold's only roll is 3.
why: Once Blue has won, another roll must not alter a team's finishing score.
rescue: If Gold gets a fourth turn, ask for a targeted follow-up.
rescuePrompt: Check for a winner before handing over the turn.
try:
1. A branch is a separate line of work in the same project. Start a Devin session on a new branch of your practice project.
2. Send the worked example about Blue. Read the proposed changes, then open the page in its browser preview.
3. Roll for Blue, Gold and Blue in order. Read who won and both scores.
4. Press Roll again after the win, then Restart. Inspect the first team and both scores.

premise: A menu can contain two identical orders. Undo should remove only the newest one.
caption: Request for Devin
before:
Make a menu order with juice, toast and fruit. Each tap adds one item. Undo takes off just the last one.

Juice 2 tokens, toast 3, fruit 1. Order juice, toast, juice.

What total does the order show when it is empty?
after: First run: The first three choices total 7. Undo removes only the last juice and leaves 5. Second run: The order reaches zero without turning negative. Fruit starts a fresh order totaling 1. 2 + 3 + 2 = 7. Removing the last 2 leaves 5.
why: Undoing the last juice should leave the earlier juice on the order.
rescue: If both juices disappear, ask for a targeted follow-up.
rescuePrompt: Remove the last list entry instead of all entries with its name.
try:
1. A branch is a separate line of work in the same project. Start a Devin session on a new branch of your practice project.
2. Send the worked example about juice. Read the proposed changes, then open the page in its browser preview.
3. Order juice, toast and juice. Look at the total, then press Undo once.
4. Undo twice more. Try Undo on empty, then add fruit.

premise: A large report has an empty page before the last group of records.
caption: Request for Devin
before:
Follow the links across my three pretend pages. Page 2 has no items. Give the IDs in order and flag a loop if a page points back to one already read.

Page 1 items A,B next 2. Page 2 empty next 3. Page 3 item C next none.
after: First run: The clean run visits pages 1, 2, 3 and returns A, B, C in order. Second run: The reader flags a loop after exactly three different pages. It does not return the partial list as complete.
why: An empty middle page can still point to the next group of records.
rescue: If C goes missing, ask for a targeted follow-up.
rescuePrompt: See whether an empty items list mistakenly ends the loop.
try:
1. A branch is a separate line of work in the same project. Start a Devin session on a new branch of your practice project.
2. Send the worked example about Page 2. Read the proposed changes, then open the page in its browser preview.
3. Load pages 1, 2 and 3. Inspect the visited-page list after the empty page.
4. Make page 3 point back to 2. Run again and count the visits.

premise: A word ladder permits one letter to change at a time.
caption: Request for Devin
before:
Build a word ladder starting at CAT. Each turn changes exactly one letter and must use the allowed list. Count valid turns only.

Start CAT, goal DOG. Allowed: CAT, COT, COG, DOG. Try CAT → COT → COG → DOG.

Which path reaches DOG?
after: First run: The three moves reach DOG and win in 3. COT is a valid first move. Second run: The first move changes too many letters. MAT is outside the list. The third works and counts as move 1.
why: A one-letter move must also land on the allowed word list to count.
rescue: If a bad move changes the count, ask for a targeted follow-up.
rescuePrompt: Show the error first and return before adding to the history.
try:
1. A branch is a separate line of work in the same project. Start a Devin session on a new branch of your practice project.
2. Send the worked example about CAT. Read the proposed changes, then open the page in its browser preview.
3. Try CAT, COT, COG and DOG in order. Count the moves the game accepts.
4. Start over. Try CAT to DOG directly and CAT to MAT, then type “ cot ”.

premise: A checklist unlocks each task only when its earlier tasks are complete.
caption: Request for Devin
before:
Make a checklist where Review needs Make report and Make report needs Read input. Clearing an early task must clear later ones.

Read input has no earlier task. Make report needs Read input. Review needs Make report.

How many can stay done?
after: First run: Checking Read input unlocks Make report. Checking Make report unlocks Review. Second run: Both later tasks become unchecked and locked. The finish count returns to 0 of 3.
why: Taking away an early sign-off must lock and uncheck every step that depended on it.
rescue: If Review stays done, ask for a targeted follow-up.
rescuePrompt: Follow the chain past the first task that became invalid.
try:
1. A branch is a separate line of work in the same project. Start a Devin session on a new branch of your practice project.
2. Send the worked example about Review. Read the proposed changes, then open the page in its browser preview.
3. Check Read input, then Make report. Watch which box unlocks each time.
4. Finish all three, then uncheck Read input. Inspect the later tasks and their reasons.

premise: Several files have different names but may contain the same text.
caption: Request for Devin
before:
Make a duplicate-file report from the sample text. Put B.txt with files that have the same contents, not merely the same size.

A.txt has blue. B.txt has blue. C.txt has gold. All three words have four letters.

What groups appear after an edit?
after: First run: A.txt and B.txt share a group. C.txt stands alone even though all sizes match. Second run: B and C now group together. A and D stand alone. The tool leaves every file in place.
why: Equal file sizes narrow the search but cannot prove equal contents.
rescue: If C joined the first group, ask for a targeted follow-up.
rescuePrompt: Compare the actual file contents before grouping equal-length entries. Leave every file in place.
try:
1. A branch is a separate line of work in the same project. Start a Devin session on a new branch of your practice project.
2. Send the worked example about B.txt. Read the proposed changes, then open the page in its browser preview.
3. Group A.txt, B.txt and C.txt. Look at their contents and groups, not just their sizes.
4. Change B.txt to gold and add a new empty D.txt. Run the finder again.

premise: A ranking board needs to keep equal results tied.
caption: Request for Devin
before:
Build a scoreboard with shared rank for ties and a gap after a tie. Mark all leaders, let me edit a score and restore the sample. Store updated scores in this browser so a reload keeps them.

Blue 7, Gold 7, Green 4. Put equal scores at the same rank; next rank skips the tied slot.

Who shares first place?
after: First run: The ranks are Blue 1, Gold 1, Green 3. Both top teams are marked joint leaders. Second run: Green is 1. Blue and Gold share rank 2. After reset the original scores and tie return.
why: Two teams sharing first place occupy two ranking slots, so the following team is third.
rescue: If Gold is called second at 7, ask for a targeted follow-up.
rescuePrompt: Compare its points with the previous team before assigning a new rank.
try:
1. A branch is a separate line of work in the same project. Start a Devin session on a new branch of your practice project.
2. Send the worked example about rank. Read the proposed changes, then open the page in its browser preview.
3. Load the three sample teams. Look at the two leaders and the rank after them.
4. Change Green to 8, reload, and compare all ranks. Then reset.

premise: A six-tile treasure board should award points only the first time someone opens a tile.
caption: Request for Devin
before:
Make a two-team treasure board that hides the sample coins and gem. Give points only on the first pick of a tile, then switch teams.

Fixed 2×3 grid slots 1–6 contain coin, blank, coin, gem, blank, coin. Coin=1, gem=3. Turns alternate Blue then Gold.

Which team keeps its turn on a repeat?
after: First run: The first tile holds a coin and the fourth holds a gem. Blue has 1 and Gold 3. The repeat leaves Blue’s turn in place. Second run: The final scores are Blue 1 and Gold 5. The new game covers all six tiles and returns the first turn to Blue. Blue collects 1 + 0 + 0 = 1. Gold collects 3 + 1 + 1 = 5.
why: Refusing a repeated treasure tile must also preserve the next player's turn.
rescue: If the winner differs, ask for a targeted follow-up.
rescuePrompt: Write down who owned each legal pick and check whether the repeated 1 wrongly used a turn.
try:
1. A branch is a separate line of work in the same project. Start a Devin session on a new branch of your practice project.
2. Send the worked example about gem. Read the proposed changes, then open the page in its browser preview.
3. Pick tiles 1 and 4, then try 1 again. Note who gets the next move.
4. Continue with 2, 3, 5 and 6. Read the winner and replay. Test all buttons with the keyboard.

premise: Two mailbox lists were taken on different days. The support team needs to see what changed.
caption: Request for Devin
before:
My mailbox lists changed overnight. Build a read-only comparison with a downloadable report. Match IDs without case; show added, gone, changed and unchanged IDs. If an ID appears twice, show an error and keep the last good download.

Before A=user, B=shared, C=user. After A=user, B=user, D=shared. IDs are pretend and match without case.
after: First run: The clean run shows D added, C removed, B changed from shared to user and A the same. Every ID appears once. Second run: The duplicate case shows a row error and keeps the last good result. The restored download matches all four expected entries.
why: Two entries for the same mailbox make the change unclear. The last good report stays available while you fix the list.
rescue: If B and b become separate boxes, ask for a targeted follow-up.
rescuePrompt: Check each ID after cleaning spaces and case but before building the comparison.
try:
1. A branch is a separate line of work in the same project. Start a Devin session on a new branch of your practice project.
2. Send Devin the two mailbox lists and the worked request. Read the proposed changes, then open the page in its browser preview.
3. Load both mailbox lists, compare them and download the first report. Check the entry for each ID.
4. Save the good report. Add a second b to After and compare. Then restore the original input and download again.

premise: A quiz button calls a scoring rule in another file. You want the rule and its caller before changing anything.
caption: Practice request
before: In this practice repo, where does a correct pick earn points? Trace the call from button.py to scoring.py. Give both file links and the score for a correct pick. Leave the files alone.
after: First run: The path goes from pick in button.py to award in scoring.py. A correct pick earns 2 points. Second run: A wrong pick earns 0 points. Both answers point back to award.
why: Two links let you tell which file asks for the score and which file actually sets it.
rescue: If Devin points only to the button, ask it to follow the call into the second file.
rescuePrompt: Trace the call to award. Which file defines it, and what does that file return when ok is False?
try:
1. In an indexed practice repo, put def award(ok): return 2 if ok else 0 in scoring.py. In button.py add from scoring import award and then def pick(ok): return award(ok) on the next line. Commit the files and wait for the index to catch up.
2. In Ask, select the repo and send the request about button.py. Follow each file link and compare its line with the answer.
3. Ask for the score when pick receives False. Check the same rule without starting an Agent session.

premise: A small score helper gives a point for a tie. You want a test and a proposed fix you can inspect.
caption: Practice request
before: Create points.py in this practice repo with a points(result) function. The rule is 2 for win and 1 for tie. Test both cases and report the output. Work on a practice branch.
after: First run: The test output shows win 2 and tie 1. Second run: The draft PR changes tie to 0. The tests show win 2 and tie 0.
why: Checking the win again catches a fix that changes every score instead of just the tie.
rescue: If the second test only covers the tie, ask for the unchanged win case in the same test run.
rescuePrompt: Show the expected and actual scores for both win and tie on the proposed branch.
try:
1. In an Agent session, select a writable practice repo and send the points.py request. Read the file and the two test results.
2. Tell Devin the revised rule is 0 for a tie, while a win still earns 2. Ask it to update the checks, run them and open a draft PR. Leave the PR open for review.

premise: A map of a small quiz mentions a separate deck. You want to see the code behind that link.
caption: Practice request
before: Using the wiki for this project, explain how quiz.py gets the first card from deck.py. Cite both files. Which word would the player see first in this revision?
after: First run: The quiz reads position 0 of CARDS in deck.py. The first word is PEAR. Second run: Position 1 contains PLUM. Both answers refer to the same list.
why: A map helps you find a file. The order of the words in that file settles which one the code will display.
rescue: If the answer uses a different word, ask for the two list items in their stored order and compare the cited revision.
rescuePrompt: Show the line that defines CARDS and the line that reads it. What are the two positions in this revision?
try:
1. In a practice repo set deck.py to CARDS = ["PEAR", "PLUM"]. In quiz.py put from deck import CARDS and then print(CARDS[0]) on its own line. Commit the files and index the repo.
2. Open its DeepWiki. Read the page for the quiz and use Ask there with the question about deck.py. Check the file links and the first card.
3. Ask which word the same list would show at index 1. An index is a position. Python counts from zero. Inspect the file again.

premise: A small change moves an equality sign. One boundary value will show why it matters.
caption: Practice request
before: The practice badge rule is ready at 5 points or more. The PR changed points >= 5 to points > 5. What happens at 4, 5 and 6? Name the value that breaks the rule.
after: First run: Scores 4 and 5 miss the badge. Score 6 earns it. Only 5 is wrong. Second run: Scores 5 and 6 earn the badge. Score 4 still misses.
why: Testing the exact cutoff exposes a mistake that tests on the two sides would both miss.
rescue: If the review says the change looks fine, ask it to substitute the cutoff into both versions of the rule.
rescuePrompt: At exactly 5 points, show the result of each comparison and the badge the rule calls for.
try:
1. In a practice PR, make the badge change described in the sample. Post /devin review in a new PR comment. Open the review and send the badge question in its chat.
2. Compare the changed line with 4, 5 and 6 even if the review produced no finding. Restore >= on the practice branch and request a review of the new commit. Check the same three inputs again.

premise: A shift report should count ready trays the same way every time.
caption: Practice request
before: @skills:tray-count Practice trays: pine ready, oak waiting, ash ready. Give the ready count and the names you counted. Keep waiting trays out of the count.
after: First run: Pine and ash count as ready. The total is 2. Second run: Ash is the only ready tray. The total is 1.
why: Changing one label tests whether the saved recipe counts by status each time.
rescue: If the waiting tray gets counted, ask for the status beside every tray the skill included.
rescuePrompt: @skills:tray-count State the rule from the skill and give the name and status of each tray included in the new total.
try:
1. Create .agents/skills/tray-count/SKILL.md in a practice repo. Start from the starter file on this page. Change the header name to tray-count and its description to Count ready trays. Make the rule list only ready trays and give their count. Commit the file.
2. In a new cloud session with that repo, send the tray-count request. Match the names in the reply with the input.
3. Call @skills:tray-count again with pine waiting, oak waiting and ash ready. Check which name dropped out of the report.

premise: A practice project needs a tiny marker file every time a session starts. Use it to tell a built snapshot from an edit made in one session.
caption: Practice request
before: Read ~/bench-mark in this practice machine. Report its complete text. If the file is missing, say missing. Leave the blueprint and the file unchanged.
after: First run: The new machine reads BIRCH. The local edit changes that machine’s file to MAPLE. Second run: The next session reads BIRCH. The saved setup still contains the original text.
why: A session gets its own copy. Editing the copy leaves the saved starting point in place for the next session.
rescue: If the marker is missing, ask for the active snapshot and the build log for the marker step.
rescuePrompt: Which snapshot started this session? Find the build result for the bench-mark step and report what the file contains now.
try:
1. In a disposable training environment, add printf 'BIRCH' > ~/bench-mark to the blueprint’s initialize step. Save the blueprint, wait for a successful build and start a new session from its snapshot.
2. Send the bench-mark request. In that session only, ask Devin to replace BIRCH with MAPLE. Check that the current session now reads MAPLE.
3. Start a new session from the same snapshot. Ask it to read ~/bench-mark again.

premise: A test reads two lines locally. You want proof the cloud picked up a pending third line.
caption: Practice request
before: In this practice branch, count the nonempty lines in cards.txt and give the last line. Leave the file as it is. The branch has a small card list for a handoff test.
after: First run: The local file has 2 lines and ends in ELM. Second run: The cloud session sees 3 lines. Its last line is ASH.
why: The third word is a simple signal that the pending edit traveled with the conversation.
rescue: If the remote count stays at two, ask the cloud session which branch and file contents it received.
rescuePrompt: Report the current branch and every nonempty line in cards.txt. Is ASH present in this copy?
try:
1. In a connected practice repo create cards.txt with OAK and ELM on separate lines. Commit it. Start devin in that folder and send the cards.txt request.
2. Add ASH as a third line on the same branch and leave the edit uncommitted. Check that this is your only pending edit. In Devin CLI enter /handoff Count the nonempty lines in cards.txt and give the last line.
3. Open the cloud session from the handoff and compare its result with the first count.

premise: A private tool should let someone count open tickets without reading a whole table.
caption: Practice request
before: Build a private Devin App with a ticket table. Tickets A and C are open. Ticket B is closed. Show the open count and a button that closes C. The button must work only once.
after: First run: The table shows A and C open, with an open count of 2. Second run: Only A is open. A second press leaves the count at 1.
why: A second press catches a counter that subtracts again even though the row is already closed.
rescue: If a second press drops the count to zero, ask the session to count the rows currently marked open.
rescuePrompt: Derive the total from ticket status. Make closing C a one-time change and show the total after two presses.
try:
1. In a practice session send the ticket table request and open the App link. Read the three rows and the count.
2. Press the button to close C. Try it again. Inspect the status of each ticket, then open Share to check who has access.

premise: A practice report runs on a clock. You need to see that it reads the current file at the time it runs.
caption: Practice request
before: Read queue.csv from the latest committed practice branch. It has one status per line and no header. Report the number of waiting rows. Do not change the file.
after: First run: Two rows are waiting. Second run: One row is waiting. Each session has its own run time and report.
why: The file changes between the two scheduled runs. Different counts show whether the later report read the new version.
rescue: If both reports say two, ask for the branch, file contents and revision used by the second run.
rescuePrompt: Which revision of queue.csv did this session read? List its three statuses and count just the waiting rows.
try:
1. In a practice repo commit queue.csv with waiting, done and waiting on separate lines. In Automations create a Run once schedule a few minutes ahead. Select the repo, check the time zone, and use the queue.csv request for its session.
2. After the first run finishes, read its report. Change the last waiting row to done and commit to the same branch. Set up a second one-time run with the same request. Check its report after it finishes.

premise: A pilot test decides whether a change can reach two more practice projects.
caption: Practice request
before: Build a small dynamic workflow that reads a pretend pilot result. A failed pilot must hold projects Elm and Ash. A passing pilot should list both as eligible. Report only. Leave both projects unchanged.
after: First run: The eligible list is empty. Elm and Ash stay on hold. Second run: Elm and Ash are both eligible. The report contains two names and no changes to their files.
why: A stopped batch proves the gate can block work. A passing pilot tests that the same gate can let work through.

premise: A practice team needs to read a file near its worker, while its code project stays read-only.

before: Practice setup: the cloud plans the job. An Outpost worker reads the sample folder. Its Git profile is read-only. Where would a file check run, and could the session push a branch?
